text: Lieutenant-Colonel Christopher Codrington (c. 1668 – 7 April 1710) was an English Army officer, planter, and colonial administrator who served as governor of the Leeward Islands from 1699 to 1704. Born in Barbados around 1668, he was the eldest son of Christopher Codrington and Gertrude, and inherited one of the largest sugar plantations in Barbados, making the Codrington family extremely wealthy. He had a younger brother who suffered from a mental disability. Codrington never married but had a natural mixed-race son, William, from a relationship with a Black woman named Mauldline Morange; William received £500 in his father's will and became a plantation owner in Jamaica. Educated in England, he studied at Christ Church, Oxford, and was elected to All Souls College in 1690, where he was part of an intellectual circle that included Charles Boyle and Joseph Addison and became known as an avid book collector. In 1693, he returned to the West Indies to participate in an unsuccessful attack on the French possession of Martinique, then served in Flanders during the Nine Years' War, fighting notably at Huy and Namur in 1695. William III granted him a commission as captain in the English Army's 1st Regiment of Foot Guards, a largely honorary post where only 16 of the 24 companies were formed; under double-ranking, Codrington held the rank of lieutenant colonel. His father died shortly after the Peace of Ryswick in 1697, and Codrington was appointed governor of the Leeward Islands in 1699. He faced accusations of abuse of power and local disputes, which were investigated by Parliament, but he was exonerated just before the War of the Spanish Succession began in 1702. After successfully retaking Saint Kitts from the French, he resigned following a failed attack on Guadeloupe in 1703, which severely damaged his health. He attempted to re-enter politics unsuccessfully and spent his later years in retirement on his Barbadian estates. Upon his death on 7 April 1710, his body was brought to England and buried on 19 June 1710 in All Souls Chapel. His will bequeathed £10,000 and £6,000 worth of books to endow the Christopher Codrington Library at All Souls College, Oxford, which includes a statue by Sir Henry Cheere. In November 2020, his name was removed from the library due to his ownership of slaves, and a plaque was placed outside to commemorate the enslaved workers held on his plantations. His will also provided £1,500 for a monument to his father in Westminster Abbey, and the Codrington Plantations and part of Barbuda were left to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts to establish a college in Barbados. Delays from legal challenges meant Codrington College was not completed until 1745 and was initially restricted to white students; it remains an Anglican theological school and is now part of the University of the West Indies. The Codrington School, first established in 1917 and closed in the 1990s, was reopened in 2002 as an International Baccalaureate school. The Codrington baronets retained ownership of Betty's Hope plantation in Antigua until 1944.
